title: Λαγωὸς καὶ ἀλώπηξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 192. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὁ λαγωὸς τῇ ἀλώπεκι· « Ὄντως πολλὰ κερδαίνεις ἢ ἔχεις ὅτι ὄνομά σοι κερδώ ἐστιν ; »
sentences.tr: Ho lagōos tēi alōpeki· « Ontōs polla kerdaineis ē echeis hoti onoma soi kerdō estin ; »
sentences.l: The hare, to the fox: « Do you really gain much or have much, that your name is Kerdo? »
sentences.i: The hare said to the fox: « Do you really gain so much, or have so much, that your name should be Kerdo? »
sentences.n: There is no verb of speaking: the Greek sets down the two datives and lets the quotation follow, and Chambry prints the ellipsis as it stands. Κερδώ is the fox's by-name, formed from κέρδος, "gain, profit"; whether she has earned it is the whole of the fable, and the hare answers his own question at the end.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἀλώπηξ· « Εἰ ἀπιστεῖς, ἔφη, δεῦρο· ἐγὼ ἑστιῶ σε. »
sentences.tr: Hē de alōpēx· « Ei apisteis, ephē, deuro· egō hestiō se. »
sentences.l: And the fox: « If you disbelieve, » she said, « come here; I feast you. »
sentences.i: And the fox said: « If you doubt it, come along — I will feast you myself. »
sentences.n: ἑστιῶ is a present standing for what is about to happen, the ordinary Greek way of making an offer. ἐγώ is expressed for emphasis, and the emphasis turns out to be the joke: she is the host and he is the meal.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἠκολούθει καὶ ἦν ἔνδον οὐδὲν ἢ ὁ λαγωὸς δεῖπνος τῇ ἀλώπεκι.
sentences.tr: Ho de ēkolouthei kai ēn endon ouden ē ho lagōos deipnos tēi alōpeki.
sentences.l: And he followed, and there was nothing inside other than the hare, dinner for the fox.
sentences.n: ἤ after a negative is "other than". Chambry prints δεῖπνος as a masculine agreeing with ὁ λαγωός, where the usual form of the word is the neuter δεῖπνον; the reading is left as printed. τῇ ἀλώπεκι is the dative of the person concerned — dinner for her.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λαγωὸς ἔφη· « Σὺν κακῷ μέν, ἀλλ’ ἔμαθόν σου τὸ ὄνομα πόθεν ἐστί, οὐκ ἀπὸ τοῦ κερδαίνειν, ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ τοῦ δολοῦν. »
sentences.tr: Ho de lagōos ephē· « Syn kakōi men, all’ emathon sou to onoma pothen esti, ouk apo tou kerdainein, all’ apo tou doloun. »
sentences.l: And the hare said: « With harm, indeed, but I learned where your name comes from: not from gaining, but from tricking. »
sentences.i: And the hare said: « At a cost, to be sure — but I have learned where your name comes from: not from profit, but from deceit. »
sentences.n: σὺν κακῷ is "with harm", the price he paid for the lesson. σου τὸ ὄνομα is pulled out in front of the question that asks about it (πόθεν ἐστί) — the Greek habit of naming the thing enquired about before the clause enquiring. ἀπὸ τοῦ κερδαίνειν and ἀπὸ τοῦ δολοῦν are articular infinitives, "from the gaining", "from the tricking".

sentences.t: Ὅτι τοῖς περιέργοις πολλάκις μέγιστον κακὸν συνέβη κακῶς τῇ περιεργείᾳ χρωμένοις.
sentences.tr: Hoti tois periergois pollakis megiston kakon synebē kakōs tēi periergeiāi chrōmenois.
sentences.l: That to the meddlesome the greatest harm has often happened, to men using their meddling badly.
sentences.i: The story shows that the greatest harm often comes upon the meddlesome, who put their meddling to bad use.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. συνέβη is a gnomic aorist, one past tense standing for what happens as a rule. χρωμένοις agrees with τοῖς περιέργοις and takes the dative of what is used, τῇ περιεργείᾳ — doing more than one's own business requires, which is the hare's fault exactly.
